faq.q1: Does MIA tell you when to buy or sell?
faq.a1: No, and that's a design choice. MIA describes what the market has done and what it's doing now. It doesn't say where price will go and promises no result. The decision to trade stays entirely yours — what the product gives you is a clean, fast reading of the structure.

regime.title: Why there is no combined score
regime.body:
Reducing nine measures to a single index would force a choice of which one matters most. That choice is an **opinion**, and a weighted opinion is still an opinion — even shown with two decimals.

MIA therefore shows the nine measures side by side, each verifiable, and leaves the synthesis to whoever takes the risk.
regime.notSay: None of these measures, alone or combined, tells you what to do. They describe a present state and past facts.

phase.title: What the phase describes
phase.body:
The phase summarises **how** the price moves, not **where** it goes. The engine derives it from two measures already shown: the **trend** and the **volatility**. A clear trend in high volatility reads as an **expansion**; a clear trend in contained volatility, as a **trend**; a directionless market, as a **range** or **accumulation**.

It is a summary, not one more measure: it is fully recomposed from trend and volatility, and the Data tab shows which produced the label.
phase.notSay: Neither the duration of the phase, nor its remaining amplitude, nor when it will change. A phase can flip on the next candle.

trend.title: How the trend is determined
trend.body:
The trend **derives from the structure the engine detects**: it is the direction of the **last break** (BOS or CHOCH) not contradicted by an opposite one. As long as no protected level is broken on a close, a bullish trend **stays bullish**. It is anchored on a dated event (“since the bullish CHOCH of Jul 24”), the same one the Maturity tile names.

When **no break** exists in the analysed history, the trend is **indeterminate** — never a fallback “neutral”. Consolidation is described by the Phase tile instead.
trend.notSay: A trend describes the recent past. It extends nothing and does not say when it will end. It does not measure the “strength” of the move — only its structural direction.

vol.title: What volatility counts
vol.body:
The **average range** (high − low) of the **last 7** candles, compared to that of **all the candles preceding them** in the window — never a fixed number. The denominator is therefore always named, and the Data tab shows the full calculation so it can be redone.

**Why it matters in SMC:** volatility sets the **width** of zones. An OB formed in high volatility is wider, and so takes longer to cross. It is a dimension, not a quality.
vol.notSay: No direction. Low volatility precedes a rise no more than a fall.

pos.title: A measure, nothing more
pos.body:
The position expresses as a percentage where the price sits between the retained structural low and high. 0 % = lower bound, 100 % = upper bound.

It is a **coordinate**. It makes two markets of very different scales comparable and immediately locates a zone relative to the bounds.
pos.notSay: Being at 43 % makes nothing more likely. Neither “mid-range so it will pick a side” nor the reverse: it is a location.

align.title: Multi-timeframe alignment
align.body:
**What it counts:** how many timeframes show **right now** the same structural direction. When they diverge, MIA shows it just as plainly: disagreement is information, not a failure.

**What the SMC convention makes of it:** many traders treat alignment as a **confluence** criterion in their own method.
align.notSay: That an alignment makes an entry safer, more likely or less risky. No one can measure that on your account, your horizon and your risk management. MIA describes the fact — the interpretation is yours.

mat.title: Structure maturity
mat.body:
**What it counts:** the number of candles closed on the displayed timeframe since the **last confirmed CHOCH**. The starting point is always named with its date: once a counter exceeds a day, “11:00” alone becomes ambiguous.

The counter resets at the next CHOCH, never on a BOS — a BOS extends the structure, it does not restart it.
mat.notSay: An old structure is neither more nor less likely to continue. No probability is computed, and no comparison with the duration of past structures is made — that would invite a conclusion no one holds.

last.title: BOS and CHOCH
last.body:
**BOS** — a break of an extreme **in the direction** of the current structure: it extends it. **CHOCH** — the first break **in the opposite direction**: the change of character, and the anchor of maturity.

In both cases MIA requires a **close** beyond the extreme, not a mere wick. That is what separates a level touched from a level given up.
last.notSay: A BOS does not say the move will continue, a CHOCH does not say the trend is over. They are dated facts, not announcements.

dens.title: Zone density
dens.body:
**What it counts:** the zones still open detected on this timeframe, split by type and by state. Each zone is counted once, in a single state.

**How to read it:** high density describes a market that has left many imbalances behind; low density, a market that has already filled its own.
dens.notSay: More zones does not mean more opportunities, and none is presented as better. Nothing indicates which will be reached, nor whether it will be.

sess.title: The sessions
sess.body:
Published **time windows**, like the volatility calendar: published facts, not market measurements.

Many SMC traders read the market by session rather than treating the day as one block. The tile places the journal’s events within that segmentation.

**On a continuous market** (crypto), the tile shows “Continuous market · 24/7”: there is no weekly open or close. Splitting the day into Asia / Europe / America hours is then a reading convention, not a market property.
sess.notSay: No session is presented as better or more reliable. MIA does not say what the New York close will do.

lvl.title: Markers, not zones
lvl.body:
These levels are not **detected**: they exist because time passes. The day open is the opening price of the current daily candle; the previous day high is simply the previous day’s extreme.

That is the difference with the **Position in range** tile, which uses **structural** bounds. Here the bounds are **temporal**: two distinct references, never the same figures.

Each price is clickable: MIA traces the level on the chart and brings it into view. In the ICT approach these markers are often looked at before anything else, because everyone sees them the same way.
lvl.notSay: Being below the day open foretells nothing about the close. A previous-day extreme is neither a support, nor a resistance, nor a target: it is a price reached yesterday, nothing more.

marketStructure.title: 1 · Market structure
marketStructure.body: The engine spots the real footprints of big flows: breaks of structure (BOS), changes of character (CHOCH), Order Blocks, Fair Value Gaps and retests. No stacked indicators, no subjective interpretation.

regimeVolatility.title: 2 · Regime & volatility
regimeVolatility.body: It qualifies the trend, the maturity of the move and the average candle range — normal or elevated volatility. What is uncertain is shown as uncertain, never hidden.

macroEvents.title: 3 · Macro events
macroEvents.body: It spots upcoming high-impact releases (FOMC, ECB, NFP…) and flags the likely widening of volatility itself — you know what to expect before the announcement, it's up to you to judge.

regime.title: Reading the market regime
regime.body:
These six measures describe the **current** state of the market, each with its source shown below it. None is a forecast, none is weighted.

The little **?** on each measure explains exactly what it counts, and what it does not say.

trend.title: Trend
trend.body:
**What it counts:** the sequence of highs and lows on **the displayed timeframe** (here H1). Falling highs and lows → bearish. This is a reading of past structure, not a projection.

**Classic trap:** the trend is not the same across all timeframes. A bearish M15 inside a bullish H4 is not a contradiction — it's a matter of scale. Change the TF and the answer changes.

vol.title: Volatility
vol.body:
**What it counts:** the average range of the most recent candles compared with that of the candles preceding them. "Normal" = within its usual range.

**Why it's useful in SMC:** volatility changes the **size** of zones. An OB formed in high volatility is wider, and therefore takes longer to cross. This isn't a quality, it's a dimension.

**What it does not say:** no direction. Low volatility can precede anything.

mat.title: Structure maturity
mat.body:
**What it counts:** the number of candles closed on the displayed timeframe **since the last confirmed CHOCH** (here, the one at 14:00). The starting point is always named below the value — a counter without an origin means nothing.

**What it does not say:** an older structure is neither more nor less likely to continue. No probability is computed here.

align.title: Multi-timeframe alignment
align.body:
**What it counts:** the three analysed timeframes are **right now** showing the same structural direction. When they diverge, MIA shows that just as plainly ("Disagreement") — disagreement is information, not a failure.

**What the SMC convention makes of it:** many traders treat alignment as a **confluence** criterion within their own method, and read disagreement as the sign that two scales are telling two different stories.

**What MIA will never assert:** that an alignment makes an entry safer, more likely or less risky. No one can measure that on your account, your horizon and your risk management. MIA describes the fact; the interpretation stays yours.

dens.title: Zone density
dens.body:
**What it counts:** the number of still-active zones detected on this timeframe.

**How to read it:** high density describes a market that has left many imbalances behind it; low density, a market that has already filled most of its own. More zones does not mean more opportunities — only more levels to watch.

struct.title: The four structure objects
struct.body:
**OB (Order Block)** — the last candle of opposite direction before the impulsive move that broke the structure.

**FVG (Fair Value Gap)** — the gap left by three candles whose wicks do not overlap. It fills progressively: MIA shows the percentage actually filled.

**BOS** — break of an extreme **in the direction** of the current structure. **CHOCH** — first break **in the opposite direction**: this is the change of character.

MIA detects, describes and dates these objects. It never says which one "is going to work".

liq.title: External liquidity: where and in what state
liq.body:
**BSL** — buy-side liquidity, above highs and equal highs. **SSL** — sell-side liquidity, below lows and equal lows.

**Intact** — never touched. **Swept** — a wick went beyond but the close came back short of it: the level **still holds**. **Broken** — a clean close beyond: it gave way.

**The distinction to remember:** touched does not equal broken. That's the nuance most tools flatten into a single binary state.

MIA will never write that a pocket will be "taken": that's a prediction, and no one knows it.

why-this-score.text: What does this reading tell me?
why-this-score.reply: This reading describes a rather bullish market. The price broke above a recent high (a break of structure), then came back to test the broken level before bouncing: this is what we call a retest. There is also an imbalance zone left by a fast move (a Fair Value Gap) between 2378 and 2381, still unfilled, and an active Order Block just below. The overall context is a bullish trend, with volatility (the average range of the candles) remaining normal. None of this is an instruction: it is a snapshot of the current structure, to do with as you see fit.

armed-retest.reply: When the price breaks a high or a low, it often comes back to touch the broken level before moving on: this “visit” is called a retest. The reading tracks the state of this retest: either no break has occurred, or the break is done and we are waiting for the price to return, or the price has come back to touch the level and held, or it has crossed back through in the other direction and the zone no longer holds. It is a structural marker that is often observed, but often observed does not mean certain: it is a description of the market, not an entry instruction.

fomc-impact.reply: The FOMC minutes are released in about 18 hours. It is a high-impact event for gold: historically, gold moves much more than usual in the window surrounding the release (from 30 min before to 1 h after). Concretely, two things: (1) any position open now will go through the event, (2) MIA flags the upcoming release and warns you in advance of the likely widening of volatility around it — for you to take into account. To anticipate the direction of the move you would need to cross-reference market expectations — which the engine does not do yet.

historical-comparison.text: What does it look like historically?
historical-comparison.reply: I'd rather be honest: our reliability tests on past data are not finished yet. Rather than quote you unvalidated performance figures, I give you no returns, success rate or statistics until the validation is complete. What I can tell you today: there are 7 years of clean historical data and a transparent description method, detailed on our Methodology page. Transparency before the promise — that is precisely what sets MIA Markets apart.

buy-or-not.reply: No, I give no instruction to buy, sell or time the market. My role is to describe the market structure and help you understand it — not to decide for you. What I can describe: there is a confirmed bullish break, a retest holding around 2378-2381, an invalidation of this structure if the price drops clearly back below 2378, and a macro event in 18 hours that can move everything. What only you can decide: whether your risk management, your horizon and your allocation justify a position. MIA Markets is a tool for understanding, not a signals service.

why-this-score.text: What does this reading tell me?
why-this-score.reply: This reading describes a market that is hard to read for now. There was indeed a bearish break, but the price has not yet come back to test it: as long as that retest has not happened, the structure remains fragile. The imbalance zone (Fair Value Gap) is modest, and the market is mostly moving within a low-volatility range — no clear trend. Somewhat bearish news weighs slightly in the same direction. In short: few elements aligned, so a cautious reading and a wider-than-usual displayed uncertainty.

armed-retest.text: And where is the retest in this reading?
armed-retest.reply: It is still awaited. The bearish break at 1.08750 occurred 4 candles ago over 1 hour, but the price has not yet climbed back to touch the broken level. The zones to watch are 1.0860-1.0868 (Fair Value Gap) and 1.0870-1.0885 (Order Block). As long as this return has not happened, the reading remains fragile: many breaks without a retest turn out to be false breaks. It is a description of the structure, not an invitation to take a position.

event-impact.text: The ECB in 3 hours, what does that change?
event-impact.reply: A lot. The ECB decision is a very high-impact event for EUR/USD: volatility (the range of the candles) typically explodes in the window surrounding the announcement. MIA flags the upcoming release and warns you in advance of this likely widening of volatility. Any position open now will go entirely through the decision — this is exactly the kind of context where the current structure, already fragile (retest not yet done), becomes even more uncertain.

historical-comparison.reply: Our reliability tests on past data are still in progress. So I will quote you no return, success rate or statistic until the validation is complete. What I can describe structurally: this reading combines several weak elements (retest not done, market in a range, imminent ECB decision). It is typically a configuration where the reading remains cautious. Transparency before the promise.

buy-or-not.reply: No, and I will be even clearer than usual: in this reading, many elements are uncertain (retest not done, market in a range, wide uncertainty, ECB decision in 3 hours). There are many technical reasons to stay cautious. But it is not for me to make that decision — it is for you to weigh your risk management, your tolerance for event-driven moves, your reading of the fundamental context and your current position. My role stops at describing what I see.

why-this-score.text: Why is this reading so quiet?
why-this-score.reply: Because most of the elements are silent. No recent break of structure, no significant Order Block, and a single Fair Value Gap present but without confirmed direction. The market is in a low-volatility range (the candles move little). The news is nearly neutral. This reading honestly reflects a market in wait-and-see mode: there is not much directional to say. It is also the engine's healthiest reading — when nothing is happening, saying “nothing is happening.” The displayed uncertainty is wide, because the situation is ambiguous.

On the current reading (quiet H4), no break has occurred, so there is nothing to retest for now. The only active technical element is a Fair Value Gap between 2358 and 2362, still untouched. The market must first break something (a high or a low) before we can talk about a retest.

On H4, that means 1 to 2 candles will be affected. If your horizon is shorter than the time until then, the event invalidates nothing current. If you open an H4 position now, it will live through the NFP — a moment when volatility (the range of the candles) rises sharply.

header.title: How MIA Markets describes the market
header.intro: This page explains, without jargon, how our indicator spots market structures and what each displayed element means. It is descriptive documentation: we explain what the engine observes, never what it would predict.

engagement.title: Our commitment
engagement.intro: MIA Markets is a tool for understanding the market, not a trading system. Our stance is descriptive (“augmented reading” level): we describe a structure, we never recommend an action.

concepts.title: Structure concepts (SMC)
concepts.intro: Our reading relies on Smart Money Concepts — a framework for reading price structure. Here are the elements the engine detects and displays.

detection.order-block: We spot the last candle of the opposite direction just before a marked move. It is the price zone from which the move started — often where significant orders accumulated. The engine tracks its state: active, mitigated (already retouched) or invalidated.
detection.fvg: We detect a price “gap” left by three consecutive candles where the first and the third do not overlap: a move too fast for all trades to take place. The engine measures the size of this gap and tracks whether it remains open, partially filled or filled.
detection.bos: We compare the price to recent highs and lows (the “swings”). When it clearly breaks above the last high (or below the last low) in the direction of the trend, it is a break of structure: the current trend is confirmed.
detection.choch: Same logic as a break of structure, but in the OPPOSITE direction to the recent trend. It is the first possible sign of a structural reversal — described as such, without inferring a future direction.
detection.retest: After a break, the engine watches whether the price comes back to touch the broken level. It tracks the state of the return: not yet returned, being tested, confirmed (the level holds) or invalidated (the price crossed it in the opposite direction).
detection.mtf: The same reading is computed on several timeframes (15 min, 1 h, 4 h, 1 day…). We display the bias of each side by side: when several durations point in the same direction, the structure is clearer. None is weighted to produce a directional score.

us_employment_situation.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' employment report counts, each month, the net number of jobs added or lost across U.S. non-farm sectors, from a survey of employers. It comes with the unemployment rate, drawn from a separate survey of households. Traders follow it because it appears early in the month and covers a broad share of activity, making it one of the first reads on the economy.

us_cpi.body: The Consumer Price Index tracks the change in the price of a basket of goods and services bought by U.S. households. It is published each month by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and expressed as a change from the same month a year earlier. The so-called core version excludes food and energy, seen as more volatile; both figures are released together.

us_cpi_core.body: The core Consumer Price Index takes the CPI basket but excludes food and energy, whose prices swing sharply from month to month. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases it alongside the headline CPI, expressed as a year-on-year change. Traders watch it to separate an underlying trend from the temporary jolts of those two very volatile components.

us_ppi.body: The Producer Price Index measures the change in the selling prices received by U.S. producers, before goods reach the consumer. The Bureau of Labor Statistics builds it from a broad sample of goods and services at different stages of production. Traders follow it because price changes upstream in the chain sometimes feed through later to consumer prices.

us_jolts.body: The JOLTS survey (Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey) counts, each month, the number of job openings, hires and separations in the U.S. labour market, from a sample of establishments compiled by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Traders follow it because the number of open positions signals the tension between labour supply and demand — an angle the unemployment rate alone does not give.

us_gdp.body: Gross Domestic Product measures the value of all goods and services produced in the United States over a quarter. The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes it as an annualised change from the prior quarter, in several successive estimates refined as data come in. Traders follow it because it sums up overall economic activity for the period.

us_pce.body: The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index tracks the change in prices of the goods and services households actually buy. The Bureau of Economic Analysis computes it from a basket that adjusts to shifts in consumption, which sets it apart from the CPI. Traders pay attention to it because it is the inflation gauge the Federal Reserve favours in its analysis.

us_retail_sales.body: Retail sales count the monthly turnover of retail and food-service businesses in the United States. The Census Bureau compiles them from a survey of firms, expressed in dollars. Traders follow them because household consumption is a large share of activity, and this figure gives a quick read on it.

us_housing_starts.body: Housing starts count the number of homes on which construction began during the month, expressed at an annualised rate. The Census Bureau compiles them from surveys and building permits. Traders follow them because residential activity is sensitive to financing conditions and often reacts early to shifts in the cycle.

us_durable_goods.body: Durable-goods orders count the value of new orders placed with manufacturers for goods meant to last at least three years — machinery, transport equipment, hardware. The Census Bureau publishes them in dollars. Traders follow them because orders precede production, making them a leading read on business investment.

us_fomc_rate.body: At the close of its meetings, the Federal Reserve's monetary-policy committee (FOMC) announces the range for the policy rate, which frames the cost of very short-term credit in the United States. The decision is published on a known schedule, eight times a year. Traders follow it because the level of the policy rate steers financing conditions across the board.

us_fomc_minutes.body: The minutes of the FOMC meeting are published about three weeks after the monetary-policy decision. They detail the discussions that led to the decision and participants' views on the economy. Traders read them to understand the reasoning behind the decision, beyond the statement alone.

us_fomc_dotplot.body: The dot plot accompanies some FOMC meetings: each participant marks, anonymously, the policy-rate level they see as appropriate for the years ahead. The Federal Reserve publishes it as a scatter of dots. Traders consult it to place the range of views within the committee, without it being a commitment.

ea_hicp_flash.body: The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices tracks the change in the price of a basket of goods and services across the euro area, using a method common to all member states. Eurostat publishes a flash estimate at the end of each month, expressed as a change from the same month a year earlier; the figure is confirmed a few weeks later.

ea_gdp_flash.body: The euro-area flash GDP estimate measures the change in economic activity from one quarter to the next. Eurostat publishes it shortly after the quarter ends, using a method common to member states, then revises it as national data fill in. Traders follow it because it sums up the region's activity early.

ea_unemployment.body: The euro-area unemployment rate relates the number of people without a job and looking for one to the active population. Eurostat computes it each month using a definition harmonised across member states, adjusted for seasonal variation. Traders follow it as a read on the labour market at the regional scale.

ea_ecb_rate.body: At the close of its monetary-policy meetings, the European Central Bank announces its key rates, which frame the cost of short-term credit in the euro area. The decision is published on a known schedule, about eight times a year. Traders follow it because the level of these rates steers financing conditions across the region.

describe.title: Describe your strategy. In your words.
describe.subtitle: No form to fill in. Write what you're looking for as you'd say it to someone.
describe.miaSub: she chooses nothing for you · you validate before anything runs
describe.placeholder: E.g.: I'm looking for an untested Order Block, in an uptrend, with the 1 h agreeing and a liquidity pocket taken recently.
describe.scope: M.I.A translates toward 22 verifiable conditions. Nothing else.
describe.disclaimer: M.I.A does not look at the market to answer you: she turns your sentence into verifiable conditions, then the product's analysis does the searching. She orders nothing, advises nothing, and never guesses a condition you didn't express.

ranking.title: I don't sort markets
ranking.body: Asking for “the X” implies an order of preference. The scanner builds none and never sorts its results. A market meeting five conditions is not preferable to one meeting three — it is different, and the call is yours.

prediction.title: I don't predict prices
prediction.body: The product describes the current state of markets. It doesn't say where price will go, nor whether it will rise or fall. I can translate a strategy that describes a present structure, not an expectation.

recommendation.title: I advise no position
recommendation.body: I don't say what to trade, nor when to buy or sell. The scanner shows where conditions YOU described are present; the decision stays yours.
